newsitem.title: USA: Maine seen with $420 mln shortfall in next budget.
newsitem.headline: Maine seen with $420 mln shortfall in next budget.

text.p: Mainly due to spending cuts, Maine is facing an approximately $420 million shortfall for its next two-year budget, a state finance official said.
But the official noted that the state wants to avoid using one-shot items to fix the budget.
Janet Waldron told a Bond Buyer conference here on public finance in New England Monday, "We're taking it very seriously."
She added, "Our commitment this time is not to look at one-time gimmicks."
Gov. Angus King plans to cut $65 million in the next budget, after cutting $45 million in the preceeding one, Waldron said.
Maine, which has around $500 million of debt outstanding, this January will work on its next two-year budget for the 1998 and 1999 fiscal years, explained Samuel Shapiro, the state treasurer.
The current two-year budget ends in June 1997.

Even if the state's voters on Nov 5 approve a $40.5 million bond referendum for environmental clean-ups, the amount the state has borrowed will remain level, he said, noting that Maine plans to pay off $77 million of debt in 1996 and $79 million in 1997.

Among the promising signs Waldron saw for the state's economy, which is recovering from the nationwide recession in the early 1990s that hit New England particularly hard, were a rise in revenues, which are four percent more than forecast.

Waldron also cited reductions in the costs of workers' compensation, which now are competitive with other states, and highlighted the efforts of Gov. King to attract new businesses. The state has slashed its workforce by 12 percent and reduced short-term borrowing.

"We've seen some real improvement in the state's cash position," she said, adding that the Maine previously had seen some of the negative impact of relying upon one-time methods of closing budget gaps. She did not elaborate on the adverse consequences of such actions.

The state official added that Maine ended the last fiscal year with a $25 million surplus, up from $4.5 million in the previous period, while its Rainy Day Fund at more than $38 million is the highest it ever has been.
